Use case: on-prem enterprise AI search with Cohere models

DOCS AND A LIVE DATABASE.
ONE CPU SERVER.
ANSWERS YOU CAN CHECK.

A worked example we ran on public data, modelled on what enterprise users ask for. Picture a mid-size health insurer: a compliance team that lives in NIST frameworks and CMS claims manuals, and an operations team that lives in a Postgres claims table. They want one search layer inside their own network, Cohere models on top, and nothing invented. We built exactly that on one machine. The documents are 13 real public-domain U.S. government PDFs. The claims table is synthetic, generated by us, 200,000 rows. Every number below is from that run; the Cohere steps ran against a mock of Cohere's API because we have no key yet, and they are labelled that way.

FOR·INSURERS·BANKS·HEALTHCARE·PUBLIC SECTOR

1. THE DOCUMENTS. ONE COMMAND.

The corpus: NIST AI RMF 1.0, the NIST generative AI profile, CSF 2.0, SP 800-53 rev. 5, SP 800-61 rev. 3, SP 800-30, the NIST Privacy Framework, and six chapters of CMS manuals on claims processing, benefit policy and program integrity. All public domain. One command makes them searchable, one record per page or section.

$ xerj autoindex ./corpus --prefix policy
indexed: 3033 documents live; this run submitted 3033 source records from 14 files
xerj-done ok=true exit=0 reason=completed wall=7.9s files=14 records=3033

Searching it: a full-text match over the 3,033 records ran at 0.8 ms p50 and 2.3 ms p95 on the same node.

2. THE DATABASE. CONNECT ONCE.

The claims table lives in Postgres 16. One command registers it as a source inside the node: a consistent snapshot, then every insert, update and delete through Postgres logical replication. The node remembers it across restarts.

$ xerj connect postgres://ops@db.internal/claims --password-env PG_SRC_PW
claims: snapshotting 92% (185000 rows, 47105 rows/s, ETA 0 s)
claims: streaming
claims is live (streaming). Indices:
  public.claims -> src-claims-public-claims (200000 rows)
MeasuredResult
Snapshot of 200,000 rowsabout 47,100 rows/s
60 single-row UPDATEs, commit to visible in XERJp50 19.7 ms · p95 21.7 ms · max 34.6 ms
A DELETE and an INSERTthe deleted claim is gone (404), the new one is there

3. QUESTIONS IN PLAIN WORDS. ANSWERS WITH EVIDENCE.

For plain-language questions over structured records, we wrote 1,000 claims (an export of the same table) as facts and asked XERJ Query-1. It compiles each question into a small program, runs it over the facts and shows the record it used. When it cannot ground an answer it says UNKNOWN; it does not guess.

$ xerj autoindex claims.csv --facts claims --key claim_id
claims: 1000 rows · key claim_id · wrote 6000 facts (1000 new, 0 changed, 0 unchanged, 0 withdrawn)
QuestionXERJ Query-1Correct?
How many claims have member_region West?200 · counting, two models agreedyes (200)
How many claims have status denied and member_region West?34 · counting, two models agreedyes (34)
What is the status of CLM-0000002?approved · evidence: the status fact of CLM-0000002yes
What is the reviewer of CLM-0000010?A. Rivera · with evidenceyes
What is the amount_usd of CLM-0000007?309 · quote "309.00"yes
How many claims have status denied?UNKNOWNdeclined (167)
How many claims have provider_type telehealth?UNKNOWNdeclined (166)
What is the total amount_usd of claims with status paid?UNKNOWN (sums are not supported yet)declined

Five answers, five correct, three honest declines, about 0.2 to 0.4 seconds each on CPU. For totals, the ordinary aggregation in step 2 is the right tool and is exact.

4. COHERE ON TOP. CITATIONS BACK TO THE PAGE.

Rerank as a stage of XERJ's own search, then Command answering from the best passages with citations that resolve to a file and a page. These calls went to a mock of Cohere's API (no key yet), so they prove the wiring and the shapes, not Cohere's quality.

POST /policy-docs/_search
{"query": {"match": {"body": "how long does a beneficiary have to file an appeal of a claim decision"}},
 "rerank": {"provider": "cohere", "model": "rerank-v5.0-fast", "window": 30}}

"_rerank": {"applied": true, "provider": "cohere", "model": "rerank-v5.0-fast",
            "window": 30, "judged": 30, "partial_failures": 0, "usage": {"search_units": 0}}
$ python3 command_rag.py ask "How long does a beneficiary have to file an appeal of a claim decision?" --assert-citations
Citations:
  -> cms-benefit-policy-ch15.pdf page 29 (_id 0ced0557c9bed8f895a9a8bb1fda8253)
  -> cms-benefit-policy-ch15.pdf page 42 (_id f503a0792638a0f359ebb1ff2702e546)

The cookbook embedded all 3,033 records and wrote them back with vectors in 7.6 seconds against the mock; with a real key, that time depends on Cohere's API. The mock's answer text is left out because it says nothing about Cohere's quality.

WHAT IT RAN ON, AND WHAT IT COSTS.

Everything ran on one laptop-class machine (x86_64). The search node, holding the 200,000-row table, the 3,033 document records and the vector index, used 787 MB of RAM. The node with the XERJ Query-1 model used 1.05 GB. For a larger example workload, 10 GB of text and a million questions a month, we priced one 32 GB CPU server at about $468 a month against $21,175 to $65,747 for managed vector-RAG and GraphRAG stacks on the same data, at list prices fetched on 2026-11-05. Most of that difference is the per-question language-model bill, not the infrastructure. Method and caveats.

What we did not test. No call to Cohere's real API (no key yet): Cohere's ranking quality, latency, cost and the exact citation format are unverified here. No private Cohere deployment. No customer data: the documents are public, the claims are synthetic. One machine, not a cluster. MySQL sources are not built yet. Live database changes do not yet flow into XERJ Query-1 facts automatically; we wrote facts from an export.
